title: The Deal Desk, episode 16: The cost of capital, or how Klarna lost eighty-five percent
hook: In thirteen months Klarna's valuation fell from forty-five point six billion dollars to six point seven billion. One of its oldest backers said the business had never been stronger. The discount rate had moved.
voice_version: gemini-3.8-flash-tts|Sadaltager|a senior London mergers and acquisitions banker in his late thirties, presenting a finance podcast; slightly lower, deeper register than usual; measured, informative and authoritative, like an FT or Bloomberg presenter explaining to a smart listener; clear and composed, warm but never sarcastic, smug or casual|Autonoe|a curious young university student; bright and engaged, conversational|chunks-v2

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: This is The Deal Desk, episode sixteen. Yesterday we learned that the tooth fairy doesn't pay for the ovens. Today we find out who sets the discount rate. The weighted average cost of capital, the capital asset pricing model, and beta. And we start in Stockholm.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Klarna?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Klarna, the Swedish buy now, pay later company. In June twenty twenty-one, a funding round valued it at forty-five point six billion dollars. On the eleventh of July twenty twenty-two, it raised eight hundred million dollars at a valuation of six point seven billion.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: That's down more than eighty percent.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Eighty-five percent, in about thirteen months. And here's the strange part. Michael Moritz of Sequoia, which first invested in Klarna in twenty ten, said the business was stronger than at any time since then. He put the fall entirely down to investors suddenly voting the opposite way.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So what changed, if the business didn't?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Klarna's own press release pointed to the worst stock downturn in fifty years, and compared itself with listed fintech companies whose shares had collapsed. Behind that downturn sat one number. In March twenty twenty-two, the Federal Reserve started raising its key rate from close to zero, to a range of a quarter to half a percent. By December, it was four and a quarter to four and a half.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Four points in nine months.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: And every discount rate in the world moved with it. Most of Klarna's value lived in the future, in profits years away. When the rate you discount at goes up, far-off profits shrink the most. By the end of today you'll be able to show why.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So the discount rate is just the interest rate.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: First trap. The interest rate is the starting point, not the answer. Remember episode fifteen: unlevered free cash flow belongs to lenders and shareholders together. So the discount rate has to be what both of them demand, blended. That's the weighted average cost of capital. In interviews you'll hear it as wack, W-A-C-C. Two ingredients, the cost of debt and the cost of equity, each weighted by how much of the company it funds.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Cost of debt is easy. It's the interest rate the company pays.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Nearly. It's the rate the company would pay to borrow today, not the coupon on bonds it issued years ago. Say Cafe Group could borrow at eight percent. But interest cuts the tax bill. With tax at twenty-five percent, the after-tax cost of debt is six percent. That's the tax saving we parked yesterday. It lives here, in the rate, not in the cash flow.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And equity? Shareholders don't charge interest. Dividends are optional. So equity is the cheap money.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Second trap, and the most expensive one. Equity is the dearest money a company has. Shareholders are paid last, after lenders, staff and the tax office, and nothing is promised to them. So they demand more. To put a number on it, we use the capital asset pricing model. C-A-P-M, usually said cap-em. Cost of equity equals the risk-free rate, plus beta times the equity risk premium.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Three pieces.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: The risk-free rate is the yield on a government bond, in the same currency as the cash flows. Say four percent. The equity risk premium is the extra return investors want for holding shares instead of that bond, across the whole market. Say five percent. And beta says how much this company's shares move when the market moves.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So beta measures how risky the share is. A share that swings a lot has a high beta.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Third trap. Beta measures how a share moves with the market, not how much it swings on its own. A small drug developer can jump fifty percent on one trial result, but an investor holding a hundred different shares can diversify that away. Nobody can diversify away the market itself, so that's the risk investors get paid for. A beta of one moves with the market. One point five moves half as much again.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And Cafe Group?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Cafés suffer when people stop spending, so say one point two. Four percent, plus one point two times five. That's six more points. Cost of equity: ten percent.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Then the weights. Cafe Group's balance sheet shows very little equity, so it's mostly debt.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Fourth trap. Market values, not book values. The balance sheet records what shareholders paid in years ago. What matters is what investors would hand over for those shares today. Keep it round: at market value, Cafe Group is three quarters equity and one quarter debt. Three quarters of ten is seven and a half. A quarter of six is one and a half. Weighted average cost of capital: nine percent.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So nine percent is what all of Cafe Group's investors, together, expect to earn.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly. And that's why it's the right rate for unlevered free cash flow. Same owners, same cash, same rate. Now back to twenty twenty-two. Take a company whose cost of capital goes from eight percent to ten. One hundred of cash arriving next year is worth about ninety-three today at eight percent, and about ninety-one at ten. It barely moves. Now one hundred arriving in ten years. At eight percent, about forty-six. At ten, about thirty-nine.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: That's a sixth of its value gone. For the same cash.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: That's Klarna. A mature business earning steady cash today barely flinches when rates rise. A growth company whose profits sit years ahead takes the full hit. The business can be stronger than ever and still be worth far less.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: What they'll ask you. First: walk me through the weighted average cost of capital.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: It's the average of the cost of debt and the cost of equity.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Weighted, and after tax. Say it properly. Cost of equity from the capital asset pricing model: risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium. Cost of debt at today's borrowing rate, minus the tax saving. Weight each by its share of the company at market value, often a target mix for that kind of business. Add them up. That's the return all capital providers require, the rate for unlevered free cash flow.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Second?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Which is cheaper, debt or equity, and why?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Debt, because interest rates are lower than what the stock market returns.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Right answer, thin reason. Lenders are paid before shareholders, often with security, so they take less risk. And interest is tax deductible. Then the follow-up: why not fund everything with debt? Because more debt makes the equity riskier, so its beta and its cost rise, and lenders charge more too. Past a point, the risk of going bust outweighs the tax saving.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Third?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: How do you find beta for a private company, or for one division of a group?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Use the parent company's beta. Or if there's no parent, one, the market average.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Neither. Find listed companies in the same business. Their betas include the effect of their own debt, so you unlever each one to strip that out. Take the median, then relever it at your target's own mix of debt and equity. Bankers call it unlevering and relevering beta, and it's the standard answer.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Deal of the day?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: A division, as it happens. Yesterday, Wednesday the seventh of October, NCC, the Swedish construction group, agreed to sell its Industry business: stone materials and asphalt, made in quarries and plants across the Nordic countries. Enterprise value, eight point two billion Swedish kronor.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Who's buying?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Two buyers in one deal. Heidelberg Materials, the German building materials group, takes the operations in Sweden and Norway. C-R-H, another building materials group, takes Denmark and Finland. The price is paid in cash at completion, which NCC expects in the second half of twenty twenty-seven, subject to regulatory approval. NCC expects a positive cash flow of about seven billion kronor.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: And how big is the business?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: In twenty twenty-five, sales of twelve point six billion kronor and operating profit of eight hundred and seventy-nine million. Divide eight point two billion by eight hundred and seventy-nine million, and the price is a little over nine times operating profit.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Why would NCC sell?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: In its own words, Industry makes standard products from fixed plants, while contracting, NCC's main business, is project-based and needs much less capital. The chief executive, Tomas Carlsson, said the sale reduces NCC's capital intensity and strengthens its financial flexibility.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: Episode fifteen. Quarries need capex, every year.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Exactly. And now episode sixteen. Here's your interview question. You're valuing NCC's Industry business with a D-C-F. Which discount rate do you use?

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: NCC's, because it's NCC's business. Or no, Heidelberg's, because Heidelberg is paying, and a bigger company has a lower cost of capital, so it can pay more.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Two traps in one answer. NCC's group rate blends a contractor with a quarry business, and the rate has to match the risk of the cash flows you're valuing. So take the betas of listed building materials companies, which happen to include both buyers, unlever them, take the median and relever. And the buyer's rate doesn't belong either. The risk comes with the asset, not the owner. A buyer that discounts a riskier target at its own lower rate overpays. If Heidelberg can afford more, the reasons are savings and fit, and those go in the cash flows.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So the discount rate follows the cash, not whoever's buying.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Nicely put. Quiz. For you listening. Question one: the risk-free rate is three percent, beta is one point five, and the equity risk premium is six percent. What's the cost of equity? Question two: equity worth six hundred costs ten percent, debt worth four hundred costs five percent before tax, and the tax rate is twenty percent. What's the weighted average cost of capital? Question three: why do you use the after-tax cost of debt? Question four: the discount rate rises from eight to ten percent. Which loses more of its value: one hundred arriving next year, or one hundred arriving in ten years? Question five: you're valuing NCC's Industry business. Whose beta do you start from?

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Pause here if you want to think it through.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: Answers. One: twelve percent. Three, plus one point five times six. Two: seven point six percent. Equity is sixty percent of the total, so sixty percent of ten is six. Debt costs four percent after tax, and forty percent of four is one point six. Three: because interest reduces the company's tax bill, so debt costs less than its headline rate. Four: the one hundred in ten years. The further away the cash, the harder a higher rate hits it. Five: listed building materials peers, unlevered and relevered. Not NCC's group beta, and not the buyer's.

lines.speaker: SOFIA
lines.text: So Klarna didn't get worse. The rate got higher.

lines.speaker: MARCO
lines.text: And the rate hits hardest at the far end of the forecast, which is where most of a D-C-F's value usually sits. Tomorrow, episode seventeen: terminal value. What a business is worth after the forecast stops, the two ways to calculate it, and why one small assumption can move the whole answer.
